discovery: Quantum cryptography: quantum key distribution based on the laws of quantum mechanics (BB84 and entanglement-based E91)

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Research, Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur K. Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84, 1984) showed that the no-cloning property and measurement disturbance of single quanta allow two parties to establish a secret key whose security rests on physical law rather than computational assumptions. Ekert (1991) independently linked key security to entanglement and violation of Bell inequalities, turning a foundational test of quantum mechanics into a cryptographic resource and seeding device-independent security. Together these ideas founded quantum information science as an experimental discipline: they motivated single-photon and entangled-photon sources, teleportation and entanglement swapping, quantum repeaters, metropolitan fibre networks, and satellite links spanning over a thousand kilometres. Today quantum key distribution is deployed in national-scale networks and remains the clearest example of quantum mechanics becoming a working technology. The 2022 Prize recognised entangled-photon experiments; this nomination recognises the conceptual breakthrough that gave those experiments their most far-reaching application.
